bib.title: News Summarization and Evaluation in the Era of GPT-3

legacy_report:
SOURCE: News Summarization and Evaluation in the Era of GPT-3. Tanya Goyal, Junyi Jessy Li, Greg Durrett (UT Austin). arXiv 2209.12356v2 (23 May 2023), preprint. The extracted text shows no venue.

COVERAGE: I read all 112,256 characters across 20 pages: body, Limitations, Appendices A–G and the example figures. I skimmed the references for origins. Figures 14 and 15 (annotator task instructions, p20) are screenshots and yielded no text, so the exact annotator instructions are unread. Page-marked text is at /tmp/goyal.txt.

CLAIMS
- claim: In an A/B study, crowd annotators preferred zero-shot GPT-3 (text-davinci-002) summaries over the fine-tuned BRIO and the instruction-tuned T0, in both CNN and BBC styles.
  number: CNN best 58% (BRIO 36, T0 8); BBC best 57% (BRIO 20, T0 30); worst: GPT3 9 / 15
  setup: 100 recent articles each from CNN-2022 and BBC-2022 (Mar–Jun 2022, chosen to avoid training contamination). 60 Prolific annotators per dataset, 3 per article, 5 articles each, US residents for CNN and UK for BBC. Annotators chose best and worst (multiple selections allowed), with no quality definition given. Scores are majority vote.
  quote: "CNN 36 24 8 67 58 9 / BBC 20 56 30 29 57 15 ... Percentage of times a summarization system is selected as the best or worst according to majority vote (may be tied)."
  where: p6, Table 3
- claim: GPT3-D2 beat the next-best system by at least 20 points, and the gap was statistically significant.
  number: ≥20 pp; p = 2×10^-3 (CNN), 6×10^-4 (BBC)
  setup: same study, paired bootstrap test
  quote: "the GPT3-D2 outperforms the next best model by at least 20 percentage points. This improvement is statistically significant according to a paired bootstrap test (CNN p−value = 2 × 10−3, BBC p−value = 6× 10−4)."
  where: p6
- claim: Reference-based metrics ranked GPT-3 below the fine-tuned models on every dataset, which reverses the human preference. GPT-3 even scored below the trivial Lead-3 baseline.
  number: >7 ROUGE-L points behind BRIO. Example (CNN): BRIO 38.49/17.08/31.44 vs GPT3-D2 31.86/11.31/24.71. XSum ROUGE-L: 41.04 vs 20.60.
  setup: 500 random articles from each of the CNN, DailyMail, XSum and Newsroom test splits. Metrics: ROUGE, METEOR, BLEU, BERTScore, MoverScore and QAEval EM/F1. Systems: PEGASUS, BRIO, T0, GPT3-D2.
  quote: "The difference in their assigned scores is very high, e.g. >7 ROUGE-L points between GPT3-D2 and BRIO. For comparison, these reported scores for GPT3-D2 are even lower than the triv- ial Lead-3 baseline reported in prior work"
  where: p8; Table 4 on p7
- claim: The common rule that a large ROUGE gap (about 5 points or more) tracks human preference breaks down for prompted models.
  number: 5 ROUGE points; 7 ROUGE-L average deficit
  setup: same as above
  quote: "large differences, on the order of say 5 ROUGE points or greater, are considered to be correlated with human preferences ... However, we find that the same is no longer true when evaluating GPT-3 summaries. These summaries score much lower on automatic metrics (7 ROUGE-L points on average)"
  where: p2
- claim: Embedding similarity barely separates the systems. BERTScore on CNN sits in a narrow band, with GPT3-D2 tied with PEGASUS and just under BRIO.
  number: BERTScore CNN: PEGASUS .858, BRIO .864, T0 .859, GPT3-D2 .858. QAEval F1 CNN: BRIO .211, GPT3-D2 .159.
  setup: Table 4
  quote: "BRIO 38.49/17.08/31.44 .31 6.6 .864 .261 .137 .211 ... GPT3-D2 31.86/11.31/24.71 .25 3.8 .858 .216 .098 .159"
  where: p7, Table 4
- claim: Having seen the reference summaries in training inflates the metrics. T0 beats GPT3-D2 on every dataset except Newsroom, the only one T0 was not trained on.
  number: none
  setup: Table 4
  quote: "Newsroom is the only one not used to train the T0 model. This further shows that access to dataset- specific reference summaries during training im- proves performance according to these metrics"
  where: p8
- claim: Reference-free quality metrics (SUPERT, BLANC) and factuality metrics (QuestEval, QAFactEval, FactCC, DAE, SummaC) also failed to reproduce the human ranking. They gave GPT-3 low factuality scores, even though the authors rarely found factual errors in its summaries.
  number: e.g. DAE CNN: PEGASUS .8223, BRIO .7577, GPT3-D2 .6671
  setup: Table 5, same 500-article samples. Entailment metrics were scored as P(factual | article, summary).
  quote: "none of the reference- free metrics we evaluate follow these trends for both CNN/DM and XSum datasets. In particular, we observe that GPT3-D2 summaries report low factu- ality scores (except XSum) even though we rarely found any factual errors in our qualitative analysis"
  where: p9; Table 5 on p8
- claim: The authors give two reasons reference-free metrics fail: some are trained on reference summaries as positive examples, and the design of the others was tuned on the errors of fine-tuned models. Scores fall as abstractiveness rises.
  number: none
  quote: "Some of these, e.g. FactCC and DAE, use reference summaries as pos- itive examples to train the metric. Therefore, al- though “reference-free” at test time, they are still trained to reward the summary properties seen in the standard summarization benchmarks."
  where: p9
- claim: Annotators often disagreed. A majority preferred GPT-3, but all three agreed on fewer than 30% of articles. The losing strong system got at least one "best" vote on more than 60% of articles.
  number: <30% unanimous; >60%; Krippendorff's alpha (MASI) 0.05–0.18
  setup: Figure 5. The extraction does not show which alpha belongs to which panel.
  quote: "this choice is only unanimous, i.e. supported by all three an- notators, for less that 30% of the annotated articles."; "Agreement = 0.05 Agreement = 0.11 Agreement = 0.18 Agreement = 0.15"
  where: p6
- claim: For keyword-focused summarization, annotators preferred GPT-3 over the fine-tuned CTRLSum (BART) for about 70% of article–keyword pairs. Preference was unanimous more than half the time.
  number: 69.8% vs 30.2%
  setup: Same 100 CNN-2022 articles with 2 named entities per article (one from the first 3 sentences, one from later). 60 Prolific annotators, 3 per article. Prompt: "Summarize the above article in 2-3 sentences focusing on {keyword}."
  quote: "Annotators pre- fer GPT3-D2 summaries over CTRLSum for approxi- mately 70% of all article-keyword pairs, showing unani- mous preference more than half the time."; "69.8 % / 30.2 %"
  where: p11, Figure 7
- claim: Aspect-based summarization gave mixed results. With simple prompts built from the TAC 2011 aspects, GPT-3 named several people as the "defendant" (a factual error), and CTRLSum failed in both cases. The authors left aspect-based work for later.
  number: none
  quote: "We see mixed results here for GPT3-D2; it generates a factually incorrect summary for the first aspect, listing multiple people from the input arti- cle as defendants instead of only “Donald Trump”."
  where: p10
- claim: GPT-3 followed sentence-count length instructions almost always.
  number: 98%
  setup: human-study test instances
  quote: "GPT3-D2 summaries faithfully fol- low the given length constraint in 98% of the test instances used in our human study data"
  where: p3
- claim: Summary length does not explain the preference. GPT-3 summaries were 9 words longer on average, but length difference correlated weakly with votes.
  number: Pearson 0.17 (CNN), .02 (BBC)
  quote: "Pearson’s ρ is 0.17 for CNN and .02 for the BBC dataset."
  where: p16, Appendix B
- claim: Fine-tuned models copy their dataset's style. BRIO on CNN is extractive and dense with named entities, while GPT-3 is more abstractive and covers more of the article.
  number: NEs per 100 words, CNN: BRIO 12.9 vs GPT3-D2 10.5
  quote: "BRIO 3.7 15.8 12.1 36.2 12.9 ... GPT3-D2 2.9 23.4 16.3 40.7 10.5"
  where: p5, Table 2
- claim: BRIO-XSum gave very poor outputs on full articles because XSum trains on articles with the first sentence removed. The authors fixed these outputs by hand through re-ranking and re-sampling.
  number: ~30% of articles
  quote: "BRIO-XSum often generates very low quality outputs, e.g. All images: Strule Shared Education Campus in Figure 4, for around 30% of the articles."
  where: p4–5
- claim: Running the study was cheap: about $150 of API spend and $1,020 for both human studies.
  number: $0.06/1K tokens; ~2600 summaries; ~$150; $1020; $11/hr
  quote: "We spent a total of approximately $150 on API requests."; "The combined cost ... was $1020, including platform costs and bonus payments."
  where: p17, Appendix D
- claim: Naive segment-then-summarize on a long document gave incoherent, repetitive summaries. GPT-3 kept a lead bias within each segment, and the authors say changing the prompt cannot readily fix this.
  number: 3 segments
  quote: "the exact segmentation of the article also dictates the quality of the final summary, and cannot be readily fixed by altering the prompt."
  where: p18, Appendix E (one illustrative example only)

LIMITS
- The authors say the study used a single overall-preference A/B design with no Likert scales or per-dimension ratings, so it cannot say which properties drive the preference.
- It covers English news only. The authors note users might prefer domain-fine-tuned models in niche domains such as science.
- GPT3-D2's training data is unknown, and its RLHF may have included summarization preferences. The metric-evaluation test sets were released before 2020 and may overlap its training data. The authors report no qualitative difference on those articles.
- The authors expect a fine-tuned model might win when a large, high-quality dataset of the target style exists. Their critique applies to datasets built by "incidental" supervision.
- Annotators were not asked to rate factuality explicitly, only told to check it. Agreement was low (alpha 0.05–0.18).
- The paper does not test an LLM as judge. It shows that automatic metrics fail but proposes no replacement metric. Aspect-based and long-document results are qualitative only.
- Dated: text-davinci-002 and the API pricing are deprecated. GPT3-D1 vs D2 was compared only anecdotally (Appendix C).

BUILDS ON: Brown et al., 2020 (GPT-3); Ouyang et al., 2022 (InstructGPT/RLHF); Sanh et al., 2022 (T0, and its sentence-count length prompts); Liu et al., 2022 (BRIO); Zhang et al., 2020 (PEGASUS); He et al., 2022a (CTRLSum); Lin, 2004 (ROUGE); Zhang* et al., 2020 (BERTScore); Deutsch et al., 2021 (QAEval); Peyrard, 2019, Bhandari et al., 2020 and Deutsch et al., 2022 (large metric gaps assumed reliable); Fabbri et al., 2021 (SummEval); Durmus et al., 2022 (spurious correlations in reference-free metrics); Maynez et al., 2020 (XSum unfaithfulness); Passonneau, 2006 (MASI); Clark et al., 2021 (human eval ambiguity); TAC 2011 guided summarization (aspects); Card et al., 2020 (statistical power, used for the 500-article sample size).

CODE (prompts, verbatim):
- p3: "Article: {{article}}\nSummarize the above article in N sentences." (N=3 for CNN/DM, 2 for Newsroom, 1 for XSum/BBC; Appendix A, p16)
- p16: XSum/BBC variant: "Summarize the above article briefly in 1 sentence."
- p16, T0 prompts: "Summarize the article below in 3 to 4 sentences?" (CNN/DM); "Summarize the article below in 1 sentence?" (XSum/BBC)
- p10 keyword prompt: "Summarize the above article in 2-3 sentences focusing on William Barr."; aspect prompt: "In the above article, who is a defendant or under investigation?"

FIGURES
- Fig 3, p3: one article summarized at N=1/2/3 sentences. Shows prompt-based length control at a glance.
- Fig 5, p6: annotator vote distributions with agreement values. Shows "majority prefers, rarely unanimous" faster than prose.
- Fig 6, p10: GPT-3 vs CTRLSum keyword and aspect summaries, with failure annotations. Good for the applications note.
- Fig 7, p11: keyword-study win rate 69.8 vs 30.2.
- Fig 4, p4: CNN and BBC style outputs side by side for BRIO, T0 and GPT-3.
- Table 4 (p7) next to Table 3 (p6) is the key teaching pairing: metrics rank GPT-3 last while humans rank it first.

PROBLEMS: Table headers are run together in the extraction, so I mapped columns by position. Table 4's Newsroom BLEU values (.14/.04/.05) look inconsistent in scale with the other rows; that is either an artifact or the paper's own formatting. Figures 14 and 15 are images with no extractable text. I could not match the agreement values to panels in Figure 5. The PDF contained no embedded instructions.
